steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a robotics/RL paper on safe offline reinforcement learning for autonomous driving. It should explain why learned driving policies fail under distribution shift, review representation learning and offline/safe RL work, and introduce our method FUSION with a list of contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- LfD and offline RL for autonomous driving; safety and generalization under distribution shift
- Urban driving is hard: structural reasoning, two challenges
- Representation learning in LfD and its reliance on perfect experts
- Offline RL / safe RL without perfect experts; still assume matching dynamics
- Our method FUSION and contributions

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Learning from Demonstration (LfD) methods have been very successful in autonomous driving, mainly because they improve the quality of the representation in an end-to-end framework. Offline Reinforcement Learning is one of the LfD solutions, and it has been shown to be better in many other robotic tasks like locomotion and manipulation. But for autonomous driving it is still not clear how safe and how generalizable learning-based policies are in different safety-critical scenarios. There is a distribution shift between the offline training samples and the online testing environments, and this makes it harder to deploy the learning algorithms online in a safe way. Prior studies show that even small domain shifts in road structures or in the surrounding vehicles can lead to catastrophic outcomes, because autonomous driving is so high-stakes.

Existing research has applied end-to-end learning-based algorithms to racing cars with success, but urban driving scenarios are still complex for the existing learning-based agents. The complexity comes from the fact that urban settings need structural reasoning in situations that are context-rich and safety-critical. For example, humans can easily adapt how they drive depending on static contexts like roadblocks or dynamic contexts like the surrounding traffic, and they often make intuitive judgments, as shown in Figure. 1. This kind of causal abstraction is easy for humans, who have high reasoning capabilities, but end-to-end approaches like vanilla deep RL methods usually fail because of the distribution shift in the various driving scenarios. They neglect the underlying structures of the scenarios and usually end up being over-conservative or over-aggressive. So under such distribution shifts there are two pivotal challenges: (i) ensuring safety performance in unseen driving contexts and (ii) balancing safety and driving efficiency.

- Representation learning in offline RL / IL
  - object-centric, safety-enhanced scene, multi-modal sensory, domain-invariant state, agile action abstraction, hierarchical action
  - limitation: assume perfect expert demonstrations; not accessible in diverse urban scenarios
- Offline RL and safe RL
  - reduce need for perfect experts; balance safety vs efficiency with non-expert demonstrations
  - some surpass expert policies online; batch RL on improved real-world data
  - but assume online dynamics mirror offline data collection; scarce, non-diverse expert data -> mismatch
  - static (road layouts) / dynamic (traffic flow) contexts differ across locales; open question
- FUSION (safety-aware structural scenario representation)
  - safety-aware offline RL framework; self-supervised causal representation learning; evaluation on human and IDM data vs offline safe RL and IL baselines

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Learning from Demonstration (LfD) methods have been very successful in autonomous driving, mainly because they improve the quality of the representation in an end-to-end framework. Offline Reinforcement Learning is one of the LfD solutions, and it has been shown to be better in many other robotic tasks like locomotion and manipulation. But for autonomous driving it is still not clear how safe and how generalizable learning-based policies are in different safety-critical scenarios. There is a distribution shift between the offline training samples and the online testing environments, and this makes it harder to deploy the learning algorithms online in a safe way. Prior studies show that even small domain shifts in road structures or in the surrounding vehicles can lead to catastrophic outcomes, because autonomous driving is so high-stakes.

Existing research has applied end-to-end learning-based algorithms to racing cars with success, but urban driving scenarios are still complex for the existing learning-based agents. The complexity comes from the fact that urban settings need structural reasoning in situations that are context-rich and safety-critical. For example, humans can easily adapt how they drive depending on static contexts like roadblocks or dynamic contexts like the surrounding traffic, and they often make intuitive judgments, as shown in Figure. 1. This kind of causal abstraction is easy for humans, who have high reasoning capabilities, but end-to-end approaches like vanilla deep RL methods usually fail because of the distribution shift in the various driving scenarios. They neglect the underlying structures of the scenarios and usually end up being over-conservative or over-aggressive. So under such distribution shifts there are two pivotal challenges: (i) ensuring safety performance in unseen driving contexts and (ii) balancing safety and driving efficiency.

Recent LfD work in autonomous driving makes learned policies more trustworthy by using representation learning in offline RL or IL. This includes object-centric representation, safety-enhanced scene representation, multi-modal sensory representation, domain-invariant state representation, agile action abstraction, and hierarchical action representation. A limitation that keeps coming up in these representation learning works is that they assume access to perfect expert demonstrations, and these may not be available in diverse urban scenarios.

To reduce the reliance on perfect expert demonstrations, several offline RL and safe RL approaches have been proposed. These methods could potentially balance the RL agents' priorities between safety and efficiency, especially when they learn from non-expert demonstrations. Some studies even manage to do better than expert policies during online deployment with these batch RL methods, which are based on improved real-world data. These works get around the limitation of perfect expert demonstration, but they mostly assume that the online environments will have the same dynamics as the ones where the offline trajectories were collected. In reality high-quality expert data is always scarce and not diverse, and this leads to a significant distribution mismatch between training and deployment. This is especially clear in autonomous driving, where static contexts (e.g., road layouts) and dynamic contexts (e.g., traffic flow) are very different across locales. How to get generalizability in unseen scenarios is still an open research question.

In this study we introduce safety-aware structural scenario representation (FUSION). The aim is to improve how well the safety performance of self-driving cars generalizes under distribution shift. Our contributions are:

- We introduce a safety-aware offline reinforcement learning framework to improve generalizability under distribution shifts in the online deployment stage.

- We develop a self-supervised causal representation learning paradigm that regularizes the scenario representation, so that the learned policies get a better balance between safety and efficiency.

- We evaluate on the offline dataset collected from human beings and the Intelligent Driver's Model (IDM), and show that FUSION does better than the existing state-of-the-art approaches in offline safe RL and IL-based methods.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Learning from Demonstration (LfD) techniques have achieved great success in autonomous driving [1,2,3] by improving representation quality in an end-to-end framework. Among the LfD solutions, Offline Reinforcement Learning has shown its superiority in many other robotic tasks, including locomotion and manipulation [4]. In the context of autonomous driving, however, the safety and generalizability of learning-based policies in various safety-critical scenarios remain elusive [5,6,7]. The distribution shift between offline training samples and online testing environments makes it harder to deploy learning algorithms to online environments safely. Prior studies [8,9] show that even minor domain shifts in road structures or surrounding vehicles can result in catastrophic outcomes, given the high-stakes nature of autonomous driving.

Although existing research has successfully applied end-to-end learning-based algorithms to racing cars [10,11,12], urban driving scenarios remain complex for existing learning-based agents. This complexity arises because urban settings require structural reasoning in context-rich and safety-critical situations [13]. For instance, humans can effortlessly adapt their driving behaviors to static contexts such as roadblocks or dynamic contexts such as surrounding traffic, often making intuitive judgments, as illustrated in Figure. 1. While such causal abstraction is straightforward for humans with high reasoning capabilities, end-to-end approaches such as vanilla deep RL methods usually fail under the distribution shift across driving scenarios, neglecting their underlying structures and often becoming over-conservative or over-aggressive. Two pivotal challenges therefore emerge under such distribution shifts: (i) ensuring safety performance in unseen driving contexts and (ii) striking a balance between safety and driving efficiency.

Recent LfD advances in autonomous driving improve the trustworthiness of learned policies through representation learning in offline RL or IL, including object-centric representation [6], safety-enhanced scene representation [7,14], multi-modal sensory representation [15], domain-invariant state representation [16], agile action abstraction [2], and hierarchical action representation [17]. A recurring limitation of these works, however, is the assumption of access to perfect expert demonstrations, which may not be available in diverse urban scenarios.

To mitigate the reliance on perfect expert demonstrations, multiple offline RL [18,19] and safe RL [20,21] approaches have been proposed. These methods have the potential to balance the RL agents' priorities between safety and efficiency, especially when learning from non-expert demonstrations. Encouragingly, some studies [22,12] manage to surpass expert policies during online deployment by using these batch RL methods on improved real-world data. Although these works overcome the limitation of perfect expert demonstration, they mostly assume that online environments mirror the dynamics of those in which the offline trajectories were collected. In reality, high-quality expert data is scarce and lacks diversity, leading to significant distribution mismatch between training and deployment. This is particularly apparent in autonomous driving, where static (e.g., road layouts) and dynamic (e.g., traffic flow) contexts differ markedly across locales. How to achieve generalizability in unseen scenarios remains an open research question.

In this study, we introduce safety-aware structural scenario representation (FUSION), which aims to improve the generalizability of the safety performance of self-driving cars under distribution shift. Our contributions are summarized as follows:

- We introduce a safety-aware offline reinforcement learning framework that aims to improve generalizability under distribution shifts during the online deployment stage.

- We develop a self-supervised causal representation learning paradigm to regularize the scenario representation, encouraging a better balance between the safety and efficiency of the learned policies.

- We provide comprehensive evaluations on the offline dataset collected from human beings and the Intelligent Driver's Model (IDM), showing the advantage of FUSION over existing state-of-the-art approaches in offline safe RL [23] and IL-based methods [15,16,17].
